qs.q: In the management of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), a prophylactic colectomy is performed to remove pre-cancerous tissue. Which surgical goal does this procedure represent?
qs.e: Removing pre-cancerous tissue such as doing a colectomy in FAP falls under preventive surgery. Curative surgery aims to remove an entire existing tumor in early stages, rather than preventing one.
qs.s: Oncology: Surgery, Radiotherapy & Chemotherapy Explained: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with an irregular, infiltrating breast mass that involves the surrounding skeletal muscle. Biopsy shows a clonal proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. The patient has a history of familial adenomatous polyposis. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Fibromatosis is a clonal proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts that presents as an irregular infiltrating mass. It is locally aggressive and can be associated with familial adenomatous polyposis, though it never metastasizes.
qs.s: Stromal Tumors: Fibroadenoma & Phyllodes Tumor Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: In familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome, hundreds of colonic polyps develop due to
o: Activation of RAS in every polyp.
Loss of p53 in colonic epithelium.
Germline mutation in one APC allele plus somatic loss of the second.
qs.e: FAP follows the two-hit hypothesis for tumor suppressors. Patients inherit one mutant APC allele, and sporadic loss of the second allele in individual cells leads to multiple polyps.

qs.q: What inevitably happens to polyps in familial adenomatous polyposis?
o: One or more evolve into colonic cancer
qs.e: In familial adenomatous polyposis, patients develop hundreds of colonic polyps at a young age, and inevitably one or more of these polyps evolve into colonic cancer.

es.q: A 25-year-old male undergoes a colonoscopy due to a family history of colon cancer. Over 150 adenomatous polyps are identified throughout his colon. What genetic condition is he most likely to have, and what gene mutation is associated with it? → Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP); APC gene mutati
es.m:
**Condition**: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).
- **Gene Mutation**: Germline mutation in the APC (Adenomatous Polyposis Coli) gene.
- **Clinical Feature**: Characterized by the development of >100 adenomatous polyps throughout the colon.
- **Cancer Risk**: Near-certain development of colorectal cancer by age 30 if untreated.
- **Management**: Requires prophylactic colectomy due to the high risk of malignancy.

ai.title: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome caused by APC mutations, presenting with hundreds of adenomatous polyps and near‑certain cancer by age 30 if untreated. Early detection and surgical removal of the colon are life‑saving.

sections.p: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline mutations in the APC tumour‑suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21. It is characterised by >100 colorectal adenomas and a near‑certain colorectal carcinoma by age 30 if untreated.

t.b: Detects number and distribution of polyps; >100 polyps confirms FAP
Confirms germline mutation; guides family counselling
Identifies other affected relatives; informs screening schedule

sections.p: The Paris classification stages polyposis by polyp count and size. Stage 1: 10–100 polyps; Stage 2: 100–1000; Stage 3: >1000. Stage 3 carries the highest cancer risk and often requires colectomy.

The primary cause is a germline APC mutation. In low‑resource settings, secondary factors such as chronic inflammation (e.g., schistosomiasis), dietary high‑fat/low‑fiber, and HIV‑related immune dysregulation may accelerate polyp growth.

Patients often present in adolescence with painless rectal bleeding, iron‑deficiency anaemia, or abdominal pain. Extra‑intestinal features include desmoid tumours, osteomas, dental abnormalities, and, rarely, liver tumours.

Key investigations confirm polyp burden, genetic status, and rule out complications. In low‑resource settings, stool occult blood and basic colonoscopy are essential; genetic testing may be outsourced.
Urgent red flags include massive rectal bleeding, perforation, obstruction, or rapid weight loss. Complications are colorectal cancer, desmoid tumours, osteomas, and liver tumours.

Surgical removal of the colon (colectomy) is definitive. Prophylactic surgery is recommended before age 20. Medical therapy is limited; NSAIDs may reduce polyp number but are not curative. Surveillance of relatives is mandatory.
Post‑operative surveillance includes colonoscopy and imaging for desmoids. Family members should undergo genetic counselling and colonoscopy starting at age 10–12.
Peutz‑Jeghers syndrome (hamartomatous polyps), Lynch syndrome (microsatellite instability), and juvenile polyposis. Distinguish by polyp type, number, and genetic testing.
Occult blood may be negative in early disease; colonoscopy may miss flat lesions; APC testing may be negative if mosaicism or large deletions are present.
b: Occult blood negative in early polyposis

faq.q: What is the inheritance pattern of FAP?
faq.a: Autosomal dominant; one affected parent gives a 50% chance to offspring.

faq.q: Why is colectomy recommended before age 20?
faq.a: Because colorectal cancer almost certainly develops by age 30 if polyps are left untreated.

exam: A 15‑year‑old presents with painless rectal bleeding. What is the next best investigation? — Colonoscopy to count polyps and confirm >100 polyps.
A patient with known FAP develops a large abdominal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Desmoid tumour; confirm with ultrasound or MRI.
During a colonoscopy you see hundreds of small adenomas. What gene mutation should you test for? — APC on chromosome 5q21.
A 25‑year‑old with FAP is asymptomatic. What is the recommended surveillance interval post‑colectomy? — Colonoscopy every 1–2 years.
A patient with FAP refuses surgery. What medical therapy can you offer to reduce polyp burden? — NSAIDs such as sulindac; explain limited benefit.
A 12‑year‑old with a family history of colorectal cancer has no polyps on colonoscopy. What is the next step? — Genetic testing for APC mutation; counsel family.
